analysis.one_liner: Requires ground beef packages to be labeled if they contain 'lean finely textured beef' filler.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Agriculture Committee without a hearing or vote, after 15 Democrats joined its Democratic sponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal meat inspection law so that any package of meat sold to consumers that contains lean finely textured beef — a processed beef product made from low-temperature rendered trimmings — must say so on the label. It was introduced amid public controversy over the product, often called 'pink slime,' which had been blended into ground beef without any special labeling. The House Agriculture Committee never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers buying ground beef, who would have been able to see on the package whether it contained lean finely textured beef and choose accordingly.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Federal Meat Inspection Act to require that a package of meat at the final point of sale bears a label stating it contains low-temperature rendered product, known as lean finely textured beef, if it contains that product [S2][S3].
This gives shoppers at the grocery store the information to know what is in their ground beef before buying it, rather than relying on industry disclosure [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Beef processors that manufacture lean finely textured beef and the meatpackers and retailers who blend it into ground beef, who would bear the cost of labeling and could lose sales from shoppers who avoid the product.

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses a single product in a single amendment, so it does nothing about labeling for other processed additives in meat, leaving consumers with information on one ingredient but not others — a gap an honest supporter would acknowledge [S2][S3].

Critics of mandatory labeling for lean finely textured beef argued the product is safe, beef, and nutritionally similar to the rest of the product, and that a warning-style label could stigmatize it and raise costs for processors and consumers; the record here contains no committee findings weighing either side [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is modest but real: a truthful label at the point of sale, at a time when the public was actively asking what was in its ground beef. The cost falls on a small set of processors and packers, mainly labeling and possible lost sales. The bill's narrowness — one product, no broader disclosure framework — limits how much good it could do, but nothing in the record suggests the cost to industry outweighed the benefit to shoppers.

outcome.mechanism: The House Agriculture Committee never gave the bill a hearing or a vote; it sat in a subcommittee until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Chellie Pingree introduced the REAL Beef Act on March 30, 2012, with ten original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day, and on April 12, 2012 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no markup, no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].
A total of 15 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor appears on the record [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beef processors and meatpackers benefited, because they could continue blending lean finely textured beef into ground beef without any point-of-sale labeling requirement. Consumers lost the chance to see the ingredient on the package.

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require labeling of lean finely textured beef in packaged meat.

for.name: 15 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining the ten original cosponsors named at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup; it was referred to its Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee and went no further.

against.name: Lean finely textured beef producers and meatpackers
against.what_they_did: Mounted a public campaign in 2012 defending the product and opposing the 'pink slime' stigma that mandatory labeling would have formalized.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors on the record were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears, and the Republican-run Agriculture Committee never acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required their product to be named on retail meat packages, threatening sales of a product blended into much of the nation's ground beef. The industry's interest in the bill ran against shoppers' ability to see what they were buying.

Packers and retailers blending the product would face labeling compliance costs and possible lost sales if shoppers avoided labeled packages. Their interest was in keeping the ingredient invisible to shoppers.
